teaser.text: Kinross Gold is a Canadian mining company: it digs gold-bearing rock out of the ground, recovers metal, and sells it into wholesale markets. To understand how a dollar enters and leaves, follow it from rock to doré, from doré to bullion, and from bullion to the bills that keep mines alive.

stock.meta_description: Kinross stock forecast: the weighted case reaches CAD39.26 in October 2029, with bear, base and bull outcomes driven by mines, cash and projects.
stock.opening: Kinross's weighted forecast reaches CAD39.26 in October 2029, a 16% gain. It hinges on mine recovery, cash generation and project execution.
stock.closing: The full Kinross memo also covers Kinross's business, its rivals, its management and its risks.

blocks.heading: Where could Kinross's shares be by October 2029?

paragraphs.text: The weighted price is CAD32.89 in October 2027, a 4% loss including dividends. It reaches CAD34.33 in October 2028, a 1% gain. By October 2029, it reaches CAD39.26, a 16% gain.

The final-date range is unusually broad: CAD15.03 in the bear case to CAD94.75 in the bull case, against today’s CAD34.46. The base case has the highest probability at 52%. The bear case carries 29%, while the bull case carries 19%.

blocks.heading: What has to go right for Kinross, and what could go wrong?

paragraphs.text: The base case assumes EBITDA of US$4,810 million in October 2027 and US$4,494 million in October 2028. It eases to US$4,388 million in October 2029. This reflects production near revised guidance, supportive but moderating gold prices and rising costs. Kinross cut expected production to 1.84–1.86 million ounces for both years, while 2025’s margin expansion was driven heavily by the higher gold price.

The bear case assumes lower ounces, lower prices and higher costs. The bull case assumes operating recovery, stronger gold and Nevada projects contributing about 400,000 ounces annually during 2029–2031. Reserve additions replaced only about 57% of depletion, so the bull path requires execution as well as a favourable metal price.

dividend.title: Kinross dividend: history, coverage and yield
dividend.meta_description: Kinross pays dividends from stronger cash flow, but returns compete with projects, buybacks and mine risks.
dividend.opening: Kinross’s base dividend remains US$0.16 per share in each year, while the bear case cuts it to US$0.12 and the bull case reaches US$0.24 by October 2029. Free cash flow was US$2,474.1 million in 2025, but dividends compete with growth, debt, partners and closure obligations.
dividend.closing: The full memo also answers how Kinross makes money, compares Kinross with its rivals, assesses Kinross’s management and examines Kinross’s risks.

blocks.heading: How much does Kinross pay per share?

paragraphs.text: The base dividend remains US$0.16 per share in each year. The bear case cuts it to US$0.12, while the bull case reaches US$0.24 by October 2029. The current rate followed a February 2026 increase, but the production reset and heavy development spending argue against assuming repeated increases.

blocks.heading: Does Kinross’s dividend come from its cash?

paragraphs.text: Kinross generated negative free cash flow in 2021 and only US$119.0 million in 2022, yet paid shareholders in both years. Those payments therefore required other resources, while the Great Bear acquisition added another major demand. The later improvement was substantial: free cash flow reached US$2,474.1 million in 2025.

After capital spending, lease payments and interest, free cash flow was $2,474.1 million. After the additional stock-pay deduction, real free cash flow was $2,461.0 million. That is a major change from the negative figure in 2021.

paragraphs.text: Kinross also resumed buybacks and paid dividends in 2025. Buybacks reduce the number of shares sharing future profits, but their success depends on the price paid. The company increased its shareholder-return target from 40% to 50% of free cash flow in 2026. That promise now competes directly with Great Bear, Lobo-Marte and other development spending.

blocks.heading: What is Kinross’s dividend yield today?

paragraphs.text: The same test applies to cash. An 8.6% free cash flow yield represents C$8.60 of annual company cash generation for each C$100 invested. A one-quarter reduction would lower that yield to about 6.5%. The dividend yield is 0.7%, and Kinross uses other cash for projects, reserves and buybacks.

earnings.meta_description: Kinross reports on October 28, 2026; production, costs and mine recovery are the key signals.
earnings.opening: Kinross’s next results are expected on October 28, 2026. Watch whether La Coipa’s recovery and Round Mountain’s mining rate improve.
earnings.closing: The full memo also explains Kinross’s business, rivals, management and risks.

blocks.heading: What has Kinross guided for 2026 and 2027?

paragraphs.text: On September 23, Kinross cut expected attributable production to 1.84–1.86 million gold-equivalent ounces in each of 2026 and 2027. Gold-equivalent ounces convert silver into an equivalent amount of gold using market prices. “Attributable” means Kinross counts only its ownership share, so it counts 70% of production from Manh Choh.

The revised 2026 production-cost range is $1,420–1,460 per ounce sold, while all-in sustaining cost is $1,850–1,900. The second measure includes spending needed to keep existing mines operating, so fewer saleable ounces spread those costs more thinly.

blocks.heading: Did Kinross keep its past cash-return promises?

paragraphs.text: Cash-return promises have stronger evidence. In July 2025, management targeted at least US$500 million of buybacks within at least US$650 million of shareholder returns. It ultimately delivered US$600.3 million of buybacks and US$752 million of total returns. In September 2026, the target rose from 40% to 50% of free cash flow, though the newer target remains a promise.

blocks.heading: What is Kinross’s revenue and profit trend?

paragraphs.text: The sequential picture was less impressive. Revenue fell from $2,407.7 million in March to $2,238.1 million in June, and operating income declined from $1,338.1 million to $1,186.4 million. Net income stayed almost unchanged because taxes, financing and share count can steady earnings even when mine-level results weaken.

blocks.heading: What should I watch in Kinross’s next results?

paragraphs.text: Kinross’s next scheduled operating report is October 28, 2026, followed by a call on October 29. Third-quarter production should be compared with the 425,000-ounce guidance, but the explanations matter more: La Coipa’s recovery and Round Mountain’s mining rate could improve even if the company-wide total does not.
